The test section had a serpentine 3-leg channel with rounded trip strips spaced 5.08 cm (2 in.) apart on the lower surface.
Eight 0.38 cm (0.15 in.) diameter bleed holes were drilled normal into the lower surface of the first leg.
The rib height-to-channel height ratio (e/D) was 0.076 and the rib pitch-to-height ratio (P/e) was 10.
Liquid crystals were used to determine surface temperature measurements and calculate heat transfer coefficients.
The overall uncertainties in the heat transfer coefficients ranged from 8 to 13 percent.
The average cross-sectional air temperatures remained fairly constant along the channel, with large jumps between the first turn and second passage.
Placing ribs near the bleed holes greatly enhanced the heat transfer by cooling more surface area and removing the separated flow near the downstream edge of the rib.
For the uniform bleed case, the heat transfer distributions were periodic with higher Nusselt numbers near the bleed holes.
Higher bleed rates yielded higher heat transfer values near and away from the holes for the variable bleed cases.
Increasing the Reynolds number decreased the heat transfer enhancement, especially for the cases with bleed.
The lowest heat transfer occurred downstream of the rib, and the highest occurred on the top of the rib and downstream of the hole.
The inlet velocity profile had a turbulence intensity of nominally 2 percent.
The bleed flow rates were 10, 5, and 5 percent of the inlet mass flow for the Reynolds numbers of 31,000, 61,000, and 96,000, respectively.
Static pressure measurements showed little change through the first passage and first turn, then a decrease through the second and third passages.
Spanwise air temperature variations were generally greater than streamwise variations along the channel.
